content:
Christian apologists put a question to Muslims about one title. If the Quran itself calls Jesus (peace be upon him) the Word of God, they ask, does it not confess what John 1 confesses, that "the Word was God"? An old Malay article in the Bismikaa archive asked the same question in its title: Benarkah "Kalimatullah" Bermaksud Tuhan?, "Does 'Kalimatullah' really mean God?"[1]

The title is real, and the Quran gives Jesus high honour with it. The question is what the Quran means by it, read in its own words and its own context.

This article aims to provide context to that question, insha'Allah, in six facts about the Quran's word kalimah. The Quran's own explanation of Jesus frames them: "The similitude of Jesus before Allah is as that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him: 'Be'. And he was" (3:59).[2]

Before Mary hears anything, the angels bring Zechariah the news of a son: "Allah doth give thee glad tidings of Yahya, witnessing the truth of a Word from Allah" (3:39).[2]

Ibn Kathir explains that the "Word from Allah" here is Jesus, "according to the majority of the scholars".[3] The Quran introduces him through John, his cousin and witness, before his own annunciation.

The annunciation to Mary reads: "Allah giveth thee glad tidings of a Word from Him: his name will be Christ Jesus, the son of Mary, held in honour in this world and the Hereafter" (3:45).[2]

The Arabic is bi-kalimatin minhu, "of a Word from Him", with the word indefinite. The Word is named as a person, Jesus, and the verse says he comes from God. It says nothing of eternity or of a shared nature.

Two verses later Mary asks how she can have a son, and the answer explains the title: "Allah createth what He willeth: When He hath decreed a plan, He but saith to it, 'Be,' and it is!" (3:47).[2]

Ibn Kathir reads 3:45 in that light: Jesus is "a son who will come into existence with a word from Allah, 'Be', and he was".[3]

The Word, on that reading, is the creative command, and Jesus is the one it brought into being without a father. The same explanation stands in 19:35, in the passage on his birth: "It is not befitting to (the majesty of) Allah that He should beget a son. Glory be to Him! when He determines a matter, He only says to it, 'Be', and it is."[2]

The verse that gives the fullest form of the title also sets its bounds: "Christ Jesus the son of Mary was (no more than) a messenger of Allah, and His Word, which He bestowed on Mary, and a spirit proceeding from Him: so believe in Allah and His messengers. Say not 'Trinity': desist" (4:171).[2]

It opens with "commit no excesses in your religion", and it closes with God "far exalted" above "having a son".[2] A reader who takes "His Word" from the middle of the verse as proof of the Trinity has to set aside its first line and its last.

The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) repeated the verse's terms in a creed. Whoever testifies that there is no god but God, he said, and that Jesus is God's servant, His messenger, His word bestowed on Mary and a spirit from Him, will enter Paradise.[4] The title comes after "servant" and "messenger".

John opens: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God", and later, "The Word became flesh, and lived among us" (John 1:1, 14).[5] There the Word exists in the beginning, is God and takes flesh.

The Quran shares the noun and none of those clauses. Its Word is created by a command, born of Mary, called a messenger, and denied divine sonship in the same verse. Syed M. Waqas sets the Quran's language beside John's Logos theology in a study of its own.[6] The comparison turns on which text governs the meaning of the shared word. A Christian reading carries John's definition into the Quran, and the Quran supplies its own.

The Quran speaks of God's words in the plural, beyond counting: "If the ocean were ink (wherewith to write out) the words of my Lord, sooner would the ocean be exhausted than would the words of my Lord" (18:109). "The word of thy Lord doth find its fulfilment in truth and in justice" (6:115). Adam learnt "words of inspiration" from his Lord (2:37).[2]

The noun alone therefore names no divine person. What sets Jesus apart is that one particular Word from God is a man born to Mary, and the Quran explains that by the command "Be".

Muslims often call Jesus Kalimatullāh, "the Word of God", as shorthand. The Quran's own phrases are kalimatin minhu, "a Word from Him" (3:45), and kalimatuhu alqāhā ilā Maryam, "His Word, which He bestowed on Mary" (4:171).[2]

The possessive in Arabic marks many relations: ownership, origin and honour among them, as in "the she-camel of Allah" (7:73) and "My spirit" breathed into Adam (15:29).[7] The relation in "His Word" is set by the rest of the Quran, and the Quran says of the Messiah that he and his mother "had both to eat their (daily) food" (5:75).[2]

The bottom line

The Quran calls Jesus a Word from God, and it honours him with the title. It also explains the title in the same passages: John witnesses to the Word, Mary is told that God says "Be", and 4:171 sets the Word after "messenger" and before the command to say no "Trinity". Ibn Kathir reads it as the creative command, and the creed the Prophet taught names Jesus "servant" first.

John's Word is God made flesh; the Quran's Word is a creature brought into being by God's command, like Adam. The shared noun is where the conversation between the two begins, and the Quran's context decides what the Quran means by it. We set out the wider case in our article on why Muslims believe that Jesus is not God. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Bismikaa archive, Benarkah "Kalimatullah" Bermaksud Tuhan?, the origin of the question here.
  2. Quran 3:39; 3:45 to 47; 3:59; 4:171; 19:34 to 35; 18:109; 6:115; 2:37; 5:75, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Qur'an al-'Azim, on Quran 3:45, abridged English translation on quran.com.
  4. Sahih al-Bukhari 3435 and Sahih Muslim 28, from Ubada ibn al-Samit (numbering of sunnah.com).
  5. John 1:1 to 18 (World English Bible).
  6. Syed M. Waqas, "The Qur'ānic Dialogue with the Mystical Theology of Logos in John's Gospel", Teosofi: Jurnal Tasawuf dan Pemikiran Islam 10, no. 2 (2020), pp. 179–203, doi:10.15642/TEOSOFI.2020.10.2.179-203.
  7. Quran 7:73; 15:29, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
